# What can statistics learn from what people write?

::: {.story-lead}
Reviews, comments, course evaluations and conference abstracts are written for
people. This line of work turns them into data along several parallel
threads, which grew from different problems: scheduling a large conference,
reading opinions and emotions, building quality indexes and estimating what
guests do not score.
:::
:::

::: {.column-margin .glance}
**At a glance**

Period
:   2019 to the present

Threads
:   Conference scheduling; opinions and emotions; indexes from comments; reviews and places; topic extraction

Methods
:   Topic models, sentiment analysis, partial least squares path modeling,
    small area estimation

Selected collaborators
:   Marco Ortu, Giulia Contu, Andrea Carta, Maurizio Romano, Qiuyi Wu, David
    Banks. All authors are listed
    [with each publication](#publications).

Key paper
:   *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 2022
:::

## The question

Reviews, comments and abstracts are written for people, who read them one at
a time. Read by the thousands, they contain information that no single reader
can see: the topics that recur, the mood in which they are discussed, the
problems that guests or students mention but do not score. Text mining turns
this unstructured material into data that statistical models can use.

{{< story-figure files="assets/img/stories/topics-1-texts.svg,assets/img/stories/topics-2-mixtures.svg" labels="1 · Texts and their words|2 · Each text as a mix of topics" caption="Schematic illustration with invented texts: a topic model finds groups of words that tend to occur together, the topics (one colour each; grey words are not typical of any topic), and describes each text by the share of each topic." >}}

## A conference program that schedules itself [2022–2024]{.period} {#jsm}

At large conferences such as the Joint Statistical Meetings (JSM), sessions on
the same topic often run at the same time, and participants have to choose.
We used seeded latent Dirichlet allocation, an existing topic model, together
with a scheduling optimization algorithm to
reduce the overlap of content between parallel sessions of the 2020 program
({{< cite frigau2022optimizing >}}).

{{< story-figure files="assets/img/stories/schedule-before.svg,assets/img/stories/schedule-after.svg" labels="Topics collide in the same time slot|Each time slot offers different topics" caption="Schematic illustration with simulated data, not the actual JSM 2020 schedule: five parallel rooms (columns) and five time slots (rows); colours are topics." >}}

::: {.big-numbers}

:::: {.big-number}
[0.058]{.big-number__value}
[original JSM 2020 program]{.big-number__label}
::::

[→]{.big-numbers__arrow aria-hidden="true"}

:::: {.big-number .big-number--accent}
[0.371]{.big-number__value}
[optimized schedule]{.big-number__label}
::::

:::

::: {.big-numbers-note}
Score based on total variation distance, from 0 (random scheduling) to 1 (no
overlapping content). *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 2022.
:::

According to the article, an optimized schedule could also replace the
traditional in-person meeting in which dozens of program chairs build the JSM
program, a significant saving for the American Statistical Association. I
presented the approach in an invited session of the Italian Statistical
Society ({{< cite frigau2022optimizingb text="SIS 2022" >}}) and, with work on
the efficiency of time slots, at a conference on optimization and decision
science ({{< cite frigau2024enhancing text="ODS 2024" >}}).

## Opinions and emotions in reviews and social media [2019–2023]{.period} {#opinions}

A study of Booking.com reviews of 619 accommodation facilities in Sardinia
built a classifier, an adapted Naive Bayes model, that told positive from
negative comments with an accuracy of 91%, the highest among the classifiers
compared. The model was then used to identify the strengths and weaknesses
of accommodation and of its destination and, through a random forest, to
predict the score of a review
({{< cite romano2019customer text="GARR conference, 2019" >}}).

In marketing research, a mixed-method study based on text mining examined
value co-destruction in social media interactions
({{< cite frau2019value text="2019" >}}). The journal article of this thread
studied problematic interactions between customers and firms on social media:
it categorized customers' comments as positive, neutral or negative, located the
peaks of negative comments, classified problematic interactions and
correlated customers' emotions. The same pattern of emotions appeared in
different interactions, with different intensities, and value co-creation and
co-destruction occurred together ({{< cite frau2023how >}}).

A chapter in a handbook of interactive marketing followed the negative
emotions in these interactions: it detected the negative comments, located the
periods with peaks of them, grouped those periods by topic and characterized
each topic by its emotions. It concludes that, on social media, value
co-destruction can be understood as an exchange of negative comments
({{< cite frau2023value text="Palgrave, 2023" >}}).

Semi-supervised sentiment clustering, which groups reviews by their overall
sentiment, is told in the story on [clustering](clustering.qmd#sentiment).

## From students' comments to quality indexes [2022–2024]{.period} {#tobias}

A conference paper used natural language processing to explain how students
assess their satisfaction ({{< cite ortu2022explaining text="IES 2022" >}}).
TOBIAS, which we developed, combines sentiment analysis and topic modeling
with partial least squares path modeling to
estimate how the topics, sentiments, emotions and moods of comments affect an
overall rating. Applied to the evaluations of courses by students of the
University of Cagliari, it gave interpretable results on how the topics
discussed, and the feelings expressed, relate to the overall rating
({{< cite ortu2024topic >}}).

## What guests do not score [2024–2025]{.period} {#small-areas}

Reviews of Airbnb accommodation tend to be more positive than those on other
platforms, so many negative experiences remain untracked. We combined
sentiment analysis and topic modeling
with small area estimation, through a mixed effects random forest, to measure
negative sentiment and critical topics in small areas of Rome, defined by
geography and by the presence of hosts and Superhosts
({{< cite frigau2024gauging >}}).

Two conference papers followed the same data source in other directions: Airbnb
reviews used to explore spatial disparities in transportation and mobility in
Sardinia ({{< cite frigau2025exploring text="IES 2025" >}}), and
sustainability-oriented self-descriptions mapped to Airbnb reviews
({{< cite ortu2025self text="IES 2025" >}}).

## Extracting topics [2023–2026]{.period} {#topics}

Two contributions work on topic extraction itself: multivariate regression
trees for topic modeling ({{< cite ortu2023multivariate text="CLADAG 2023" >}})
and precision-oriented semantic filtering for extracting latent topics from
multilingual texts ({{< cite ortu2026precision text="IFCS 2026" >}}).
